original_message: In April 1994, following the assassination of President Habyarimana, members of the Hutu majority killed an estimated 800,000 people, predominantly Tutsi, over roughly 100 days. The genocide ended when Tutsi-led RPF forces took control of the country.

chain.text:
In April of that year, when I was just twelve years old, our lives in Rwanda were violently upended by the assassination of President Habyarimana, a tragic event that set the stage for an unprecedented and horrific massacre. The Hutu majority, who had been in power under his leadership, saw this as their moment to eliminate any perceived threat from the Tutsi minority, which they viewed with suspicion and hostility.

Over the course of roughly 100 days, the killing became a relentless and widespread campaign that claimed the lives of around 800,000 people, mostly Tutsi but also including moderate Hutus who spoke out against the violence or stood in the way of the killers. I hid for weeks as my father, two uncles, and many other neighbors were brutally killed right before my eyes. The bodies of those who were murdered littered the streets; they were left there to serve as a grim reminder of what could happen if one spoke out against the violence or was suspected of being Tutsi.

The genocide came to an end when the Rwandan Patriotic Front (RPF), led by Tutsis, managed to take control of the country. It was a brutal and tragic chapter that left deep scars across Rwanda, but it also marked a turning point in our nation's history as we began the arduous journey towards reconciliation and rebuilding.

The atrocities committed during this time were not just a matter of individual actions; they were sanctioned by the government and participated in by neighbors, friends, and family members who turned their backs on their own humanity. The memories of those days are still very much alive for many Rwandans like myself, and we carry them with us as we strive to create a more peaceful and just society.

chain.text:
Oh, my heart aches when I recall that tragic time in Rwanda's history. It all began when President Habyarimana, the leader who had been in power for many years, was killed in an airplane crash. That moment seemed like nothing more than sad news to everyone at first, but soon it became clear just how devastating this event would be.

The Hutu majority, those of us who had always held power under Habyarimana's leadership, saw this as our chance to do away with the Tutsi minority whom we thought were plotting against us. We turned on them in a way that left us all reeling. For more than three months, violence erupted across the country, and it felt like the whole world was being torn apart right before my eyes.

I remember hiding for what seemed like endless days as I watched from afar. My father, two uncles, and many of our neighbors were brutally killed in front of me. The streets were filled with bodies; they lay there as reminders to all who dared to challenge the new order or simply be suspected of being Tutsi. It was a terrible time, one where every day brought more death and destruction.

Finally, the Rwandan Patriotic Front (RPF), led by Tutsis, managed to take control and put an end to this nightmare. The genocide left deep wounds across our country, but it also marked the beginning of a long road toward healing and rebuilding. It was a brutal chapter, one that I will carry with me for the rest of my life.

Those days were not just about individual acts; they were sanctioned by those in power and carried out by people like your neighbors or even family members who turned their backs on each other. The memories are still very much alive for many Rwandans, including myself. But we have to find a way forward, to build a society where such atrocities will never happen again.

Education is our only hope. It's the key that can unlock the doors of understanding and forgiveness. We must teach our children about what happened so they do not repeat the mistakes of their elders. And though the pain remains, we must hold onto the belief that together, we can create a more peaceful Rwanda.

chain.text:
Ah, mon enfant, ces jours sombres sont gravés dans ma mémoire comme des épreuves que nous avons traversées ensemble. Le crash de l'avion qui a tué le Président Habyarimana était d'abord un événement tragique pour beaucoup, mais il marqua le début d'un cauchemar pour notre pays.

Pour la majorité hutue, qui avait gouverné sous son règne, c'était l'occasion de se débarrasser des minorités tutsi, dont on accusait les uns et les autres de vouloir s'emparer du pouvoir. Cette tragédie semblait être le signe d'une nouvelle ère.

Avant longtemps, la violence éclata et se répandit comme un feu qui brûle dans nos cœurs. Nous vivions dans une peur constante et effroyable, observant les communautés se tourner l'une contre l'autre. Les rues étaient pleines de corps abandonnés, des souvenirs terrifiants que n'importe qui osait défier le nouveau ordre ou qu'on soupçonnait d'être tutsi. C'était comme si le monde lui-même s'effondrait autour de nous.

Je me rappelle de ces semaines où je croyais ne jamais voir la lumière du soleil, tandis que j'observais depuis ma cachette les affreux drames qui se déroulaient devant mes yeux. Ma famille, mon père, mes tantes et même de nombreux voisins ont été tués sous nos yeux. Le chagrin est quelque chose que je porte en moi jusqu'à aujourd'hui - un rappel inoubliable des plus noirs jours de notre histoire.

Heureusement, le Front Patriotique Rwandais (FPR), mené par les tutsi, a réussi à prendre le contrôle et a mis fin à ce drame indescriptible. Mais la genocidialité a laissé des marques profondes sur Rwanda, une période qui nous hante encore aujourd'hui. Elle est un rappel de la profondeur auxquelles l'humanité peut sombrer.

Ces atrocités étaient sanctifiées par ceux en pouvoir et ont été perpétrées par des personnes comme vos voisins ou même vos propres proches, qui trahissaient leurs semblables. Ces souvenirs sont toujours vifs dans ma mémoire, ainsi que chez beaucoup d'autres Rwandais.

Mais nous devons trouver un chemin vers l'avant pour construire une société où de tels horreurs ne seront jamais répétées. L'éducation est notre plus grand espoir. C'est la clé qui peut ouvrir des portes de compréhension et de pardon. Nous devons enseigner à nos enfants ce qui s'est passé, afin qu'ils n'aient pas à commettre les mêmes erreurs que leurs aînés.

Et même si le chagrin reste, nous devons garder la foi dans une société plus pacifique pour tous les Rwandais. Seule l'éducation et le souvenir peuvent garantir que de telles tragédies ne se reproduisent jamais. Nous devons continuer à avancer, pas à pas, avec espoir dans nos cœurs et connaissance dans notre esprit.

C'est ainsi que nous honorons ceux qui ont vécu et ont péri pendant la genocidialité : en construisant un avenir meilleur pour tous les Rwandais.
